result:
Rain has a way of rewriting a city. Before it falls, the streets hold their arguments: buses grumbling, bicycles threading through gaps, shopkeepers stacking crates under awnings. Then the sky lowers, and everything becomes softer, more honest. Even the loudest corners seem briefly shy. Pavement turns into dark mirrors. Leaves lift their faces as if applauding. People hurry beneath umbrellas, each one a small moving roof, and for a moment the whole neighborhood shares a private rhythm.

I like watching rain from a window because it asks nothing of me. It requires no explanations or plans. It arrives, fills gutters, drums on tin roofs, and leaves the smell of wet stone and grass. There is mercy in ordinary persistence. The world is cleaned without being judged. Even grief feels less permanent under such gray.

Inside, tea steeps; the clock seems less urgent. A book lies open, forgotten. Thoughts that felt sharp earlier become rounded by distance. Storms inspire letters, confessions, long walks, and new beginnings. They interrupt certainty and remind us change can be gentle when loud.

When rain stops, light returns through broken clouds. Puddles tremble with reflected windows. Children jump in, turning inconvenience into play. Somewhere a bird tests its voice. The city resumes its noise, not quite the same. It carries a hush underneath, as if remembering how to listen.

That is the quiet lesson of weather: we are never separate from the world. Rain enters our streets, cups, memories, and stays long after the sky clears.

Rain has a way of rewriting a city. Before it falls, the streets hold their arguments: buses grumbling, bicycles threading through gaps, shopkeepers stacking crates under awnings. Then the sky lowers, and everything becomes softer, more honest. Pavement turns into dark mirrors. Leaves lift their faces as if applauding. People hurry beneath umbrellas, each one a small moving roof, and for a moment the whole neighborhood shares a private rhythm.

I like watching rain from a window because it asks nothing of me. It requires no explanations or plans. It arrives, fills gutters, drums on tin roofs, and leaves the smell of wet stone and grass. There is mercy in ordinary persistence. The world is cleaned without being judged.

Inside, tea steeps; the clock seems less urgent. A book lies open, forgotten. Thoughts that felt sharp earlier become rounded by distance. Storms inspire letters, confessions, long walks, and new beginnings. They interrupt certainty and remind us change can be gentle when loud.

When rain stops, light returns through broken clouds. Puddles tremble with reflected windows. Children jump in, turning inconvenience into play. Somewhere a bird tests its voice. The city resumes its noise, not quite the same. It carries a hush underneath, as if remembering how to listen.

That is the quiet lesson of weather: we are never separate from the world. Rain enters our streets, cups, memories, and stays long after the sky clears.
